response.answer: The fully superconducting MgB₂ stator coil is identified as requiring an MgB₂ filament with an Nb reaction barrier and Cu/Cu–Ni sheath materials. To reduce AC losses, the design must use smaller filaments, twist the wire with a reduced twist pitch, and increase the resistivity of the sheath and reaction-barrier materials. The ultimately targeted filament diameter is 10 microns or less.

response.answer: NEAT begins at 125 kW, corresponding to the smallest meaningful Gulfstream G150 powertrain with 16 propulsors. As propulsors are added or enhanced, the facility can increase total power to as much as 24 MW by using its existing 6-MW substation with load regeneration. The development path proceeds through four phases: commercial state-of-the-art component testing; ambient-temperature research hardware; cryogenically cooled research hardware; and finally integrated powertrain thermal-management hardware. In the final phase, thermal management is developed at the system level to provide cryogenic temperatures to some or all components. Across all phases, it must prevent overheating and keep superconducting components within their material-dependent operating range of 20–65 K.

claims.text: NEAT initially operates at 125 kW because that is the power level of the smallest meaningful Gulfstream G150 powertrain system, comprising 16 propulsors; as propulsors are added or enhanced, the overall level may rise to 24 MW using the existing 6-MW substation with load regeneration.
Phase 1, scheduled for FY16–FY17, uses commercially available state-of-the-art components to simulate an electrically powered aircraft and validate integration of the facility and test hardware.

Phase 2, scheduled for FY18–FY19, inserts higher-performing research hardware such as megawatt-class motor/generators and rectifier/inverters into the test bed, operating at standard temperature and pressure while targeting higher efficiency and lower mass.
Phase 3, scheduled for FY20–FY21, introduces cryogenically cooled components, initially cooled with liquid hydrogen or liquid natural gas; cryocoolers may later lift heat to liquid nitrogen.
Phase 4, scheduled for FY21–FY22, develops system-level thermal management for the complete powertrain, capable of providing cryogenic temperatures to some or all components.

Thermal management is important throughout testing to prevent overheating and, for cryogenic components, to keep superconducting subcomponents in their operating range, which varies from 20 to 65 K depending on the superconducting material.

It also allows propeller speed to be reduced without slowing and enlarging the motor, helping avoid a propulsive-efficiency penalty when noise limits propeller tip speed. response.answer: PT-2 improved measured specific torque from 20 Nm/kg for PT-1 to a preliminary 44.7 Nm/kg—more than double—through several coordinated changes. Custom annular-wedge magnets reduced gaps between adjacent magnets, especially in the sun; a redesigned modulator containment structure reduced the modulator-to-ring gap; and the Halbach arrays produced greater specific flux by using six rather than four magnets per array along with radially thinner, circumferentially shorter, higher-pole-count arrays. Thinner pole pieces further improved flux coupling while reducing mass. Further improvement remains mechanically constrained because the minimum achievable magnetic gap is governed by the mechanical design, so features that permit thinner gaps are needed.

The design goals were a fivefold increase in high-speed cruise efficiency, zero in-flight carbon emissions, and quieter flight for the community on the ground.

Thus, SABERS targets battery materials and architecture, while SPARRCI targets monitoring, prediction, and operational safety.

claims.text: SABERS proposes a solid-state bipolar battery stack based on novel Li-S/Se chemistry and a non-flammable electrolyte to enhance rechargeability and safety for UAM.

The projects differ in emphasis: SABERS develops the battery’s chemistry and physical architecture, whereas SPARRCI develops sensor-based monitoring and predictive safety methods.

response.answer: HEATheR’s thermal-management approach has two elements: (1) minimize thermal load by reducing electric-machine and converter losses and the number of conversion steps, and (2) provide local, passive thermal management by transferring heat from electrical components to the aircraft’s outer mold line (OML) and rejecting it through the OML skin. response.answer: The thermal management system (TMS) was solved separately because solving the full electric aircraft propulsion (EAP) system simultaneously caused errors in the calculated electrical losses. Those errors directly affected the TMS fluid mass-flow and temperature calculations, making system convergence unstable. The core EAP system was therefore solved first, and the TMS was solved afterward using the resulting constant electrical losses. This sequencing greatly improved stability by decoupling the TMS calculation from changing electrical-loss values during convergence.

Solving the core EAP system first and the TMS afterward allowed the TMS to use constant electrical losses, greatly improving simulation-solving stability.

Hardware-in-the-Loop (HIL) test performed at the NASA Electric Aircraft Testbed (NEAT) during the summer of 2022. The test demonstrates the feasibility and performance of an advanced energy management control strategy by integrating a simulated turbofan engine with scaled electro-mechanical hardware. A full-scale real-time reference model of a geared turbofan was run alongside a scaled electro-mechanical system representing the electrified turbofan components operating at a megawatt-scale power level. The model was interfaced with the hardware through a novel closed-loop control and scaling algorithm that emulated the dynamic speed and torque response of the turbofan shafts. The control strategy was implement ed on the electrical machines connected to the emulated turbomachinery shafts. The results from the testbed are compared against simulations that predict the testbed and geared turbofan model operation. The energy management control strategy successfully change d the operating point of the engine model and improve d its stability during throttle transients. These results also demonstrate the success of the novel closed loop control and scaling approach for emulating turbomachinery and elevate the Technology Readiness Level (TRL) of the energy management control strategy. Speed feedback is low-pass filtered to reject noise, supporting cleaner controller and HIL measurements. Mission profiles, which define the aircraft state and flight characteristics throughout various phases of flight, are an important component of aircraft conceptual design. These defined characteristics serve as sizing requirements design constraints. By defining the mission profiles to be within airworthiness certification standards and regulations, aircraft designers can ensure the concept is developed within compliance of these regulations throughout the design process. This paper presents mission profiles for the SUSAN Electrofan aircraft, including the basis for defining the characteristics required during each phase of flight. I. Introduction As novel aircraft configurations and associated technologies are developed, the planned mission goals serve an important role in determining the requirements the design must meet. The identified mission, including the design and the economic mission lengths, as well as the aircraft class, are essential in establishing the size, endurance and range of the aircraft. However, with any aircraft, off-nominal mission profiles, such as those accounting for engine failures, also have a dramatic effect on the aircraft sizing. For novel aircraft designs, the off-nominal mission profiles can have an even greater impact. In recent years, conceptual aircraft design has required increasingly detailed modeling of flight and mission profiles to support sizing analysis and design optimization studies [1–3]. While cruise conditions are an important sizing point, other aspects of the mission profile (such as takeoff and climb) and off-nominal mission profiles often are the bounding factors in aircraft design optimization [1,2]. For the SUbsonic Single Aft eNgine (SUSAN) aircraft, identifying and defining these mission profiles and flight regimes is particularly important. Research has also been conducted to better understandhowtobestutilizethesemissionprofilesthroughouttheconceptualdesignprocess,particularlyforshort-haul aircraft [1, 2, 4]. NASA has experience studying advanced hybrid electric concepts, including the Single-Aisle Turboelectric Aircraft with Aft Boundary Layer Propulsion (STARC-ABL), which utilizes hybrid electric propulsion and boundary-layer ingestion to reduce fuel consumption [5]. Defining mission profiles and requirements can also aid in the airworthiness certification approach during conceptual design, by ensuring that predicted design performance is compliant with established regulations and standards [6]. The aircraft would climb at a reduced rate and then cruise at reduced altitude and speed, allowing a safe landing within a maximum 300-nautical-mile range. For preliminary OEI sizing, the electric engines are required to provide 7.2 MW throughout the climb to safe altitude. This is not simply 65% of the normal power: the 65/35 split describes cruise thrust—65% from the distributed electric propulsion system and 35% from the turbofan—whereas the OEI case assumes the turbofan is unavailable and requires the electric system to supply the full 7.2 MW. The 7.2 MW value comes from taking half of the estimated 14.4 MW, 100%-power normal climb requirement derived from the Boeing 737 MAX 8 comparison. The sizing conservatively uses 100% power, although actual OEI maximum-continuous power may be lower because of engine limitations; the applicable OEI criteria and additional electric-propulsion failure cases would require regulatory agreement and demonstration.

evidence.text: Electrified Aircraft Propulsion Controls Hardware Testing Joseph W. Connolly∗, Donald L. Simon†, Dennis E. Culley‡, Jonah Sachs-Wetstone§, Keith Hunker¶, Santino Bianco‖, and Joseph Haglage∗∗ NASA Glenn Research Center, Cleveland, OH, 44135 Mark Bell††, Marcus Horning‡‡, Halle Buescher§§ HX5, Brookpark, OH, 44142 Electrified Aircraft Propulsion (EAP) systems hold potential for the reduction of aircraft fuel burn and emissions. To realize this potential for single-aisle aircraft, control technology challenges associated with EAP designs are increasing the demand for Hardware-In-the-Loop (HIL) studies that address the tightly coupled electrical powertrain and turbofan propulsion systems. Reconfigurable HIL testbeds enable the study of integrated supervisory control and control approaches that augment engine shaft torques to improve performance. This paper presents an overview of conceptual EAP controls architecture testing in two HIL testbeds. The NASA Electric Aircraft Testbed provides the ability for megawatt class electric powertrain testing for technology maturation. A 100 kilowatt testbed, the Hybrid Propulsion Emulation Rig, allows for rapid controls technology trade studies. In both testbeds, controls testing is performed by implementing the electrical power system in hardware while turbomachinery is emulated via electric machines that are commanded by a real-time model and controls. A novel scaling algorithm is applied to emulate the inertial loads of the turbomachinery that causes the electric machines to respond in a fashion similar to that of the full-scale propulsion system they represent. Results demonstrate desired control performance at both testbed scales for the conceptual EAP architecture. I. Introduction T he need for aviation to reduce its environmental impact is pushing the industry to explore Electrified Aircraft Propulsion (EAP) technologies for the next generation of aircraft [1, 2]. T he need for aviation to reduce its environmental impact is pushing the industry to explore Electrified Aircraft Propulsion (EAP) technologies for the next generation of aircraft [1, 2]. The dominant source of emissions in the aviation market is from single-aisle aircraft [3, 4]. While there is a goal for zero emissions, for larger aircraft a hybrid design provides an intermediate step towards electrification that addresses the high energy demands and current limitations in the energy density, weight, and volume of electric energy storage devices. EAP presents both new design flexibility and new design challenges. One of the important enabling technologies for the maturation of EAP is system-level controls technology. Control systems will play a vital role in ensuring the optimal integration of electrical powertrains with turbomachinery hardware [5]. For these reasons, new approaches that introduce control technology earlier in design phase are needed. Turbomachinery generally has a high cost-to-operate and complexities related to its operation. Implementing an untested electro-mechanical power system and its control on turbomachinery increases the financial and safety risk associated with testing. Hardware-In-the-Loop (HIL) testing is a means to bridge the gap between conceptual simulations and full-scale system hardware testing [6, 7]. To support EAP technology development, HIL facilities are beingdevelopedattheNationalAeronauticsandSpaceAdministration(NASA)tosupporttestingofelectricalhardware, control algorithms, and the integration of propulsion systems with electrical powertrains. response.answer: SMICS lets the smaller HyPER or NEAT electric machines reproduce the dynamic torque response of full-scale turbomachinery shafts by combining signal scaling with closed-loop shaft-speed control. Full-scale commands and sub-scale feedback signals are scaled so the electric machines remain within their power capability. Because the machines differ from turbomachinery in angular inertia and viscous friction, SMICS modifies their dynamic response so they behave as a scaled representation of the full-scale shaft. The controller uses commanded shaft speed in closed loop and applies torque, inertia, and power scaling to adjust engine torque and speed to achievable levels.

response.answer: NASA’s T-MATS is primarily a modular thermodynamic modeling framework for building dynamic simulations, especially custom component-level models of jet engines and turbomachinery. EMTAT is primarily a physics-based package for modeling electrical power flow and thermal behavior. Because EMTAT is compatible with T-MATS, the tools are intended to be used together to model the coupled thermodynamic, electrical, and thermal behavior relevant to electrified aircraft propulsion and its controls.

claims.text: T-MATS provides modular thermodynamic dynamic simulations and supports custom component-level models of jet engines; although developed for turbomachinery, it has also been used for applications such as fuel-cell modeling.
EMTAT provides power-flow and physics-based electrical and thermal modeling and is compatible with T-MATS.
Their compatibility supports combined modeling of the thermodynamic, electrical, and thermal subsystems involved in electrified aircraft propulsion studies.

response.answer: NASA’s SMICS enables testing in facilities such as NEAT and HyPER, which lack gas-turbine-engine turbomachinery, by replacing the physical turbomachinery and rotors with an electric-machine-based system, closed-loop control, a scaling algorithm, and a full-scale turbomachinery/rotor model. The scaling approach reduces the electromechanical hardware requirements so off-the-shelf, sub-scale components can be used while still testing full-scale electrified-aircraft-propulsion control algorithms. Its implementation uses electric machines and motor controllers, regenerative dynamic loading, power and energy-storage equipment, and models/control functions that emulate gas-turbine behavior and rotor inertia and dynamics.

claims.text: NEAT and HyPER lack gas-turbine-engine turbomachinery; SMICS replaces the turbomachinery and rotors with electric machines, closed-loop control, a scaling algorithm, and a full-scale turbomachinery/rotor model.
SMICS scales down the electromechanical system requirements, allowing off-the-shelf sub-scale electromechanical hardware to test full-scale electrified-aircraft-propulsion control algorithms.

The depicted implementation includes electric machines with motor controllers, a regenerative dynamic load, power supplies, supercapacitor energy storage, and an engine-plant inertia model used within the emulation and control setup.

The turbomachinery model and control, together with the inertia model and closed-loop scaling approach, provide the modeled gas-turbine and rotor-dynamic behavior needed in place of physical turbomachinery.

response.answer: TEEM supports transient operability by using electric machines to add or remove torque from the engine shafts, with a supercapacitor supplying or absorbing the associated energy. Its intermittent, short-duration operation improves minimum high-pressure-compressor surge margin during acceleration while reducing peak turbine-inlet temperature. In STARC-ABL, a common throttle command is sent to both turbofans, while the tailfan receives a synthesized throttle based on average turbofan speed; this provides coordinated transient control while simplifying the turbofan controllers to single-input/single-output problems. MPC could extend this approach by coordinating engine torque, tailfan operation, and energy management over a prediction horizon, while reversionary logic could mitigate failures by updating power, acceleration, variable-bleed-valve, and fuel schedules to preserve compressor operability and symmetric acceleration.

claims.text: TEEM uses electric machines to add or remove torque from one or both turbine-engine shafts, with an electrical storage device—likely a supercapacitor—supplying or absorbing the resulting energy.

During an acceleration transient, TEEM improved minimum high-pressure-compressor surge margin by 6–7%, reduced peak turbine-inlet temperature, and operated only for short periods on an intermittent basis.

STARC-ABL applies the same throttle command to both turbofans and calculates a synthesized tailfan throttle as a function of average turbofan speed, simplifying turbofan control to a single-input/single-output problem suitable for classical linear-control techniques.

MPC could extend coordinated transient and energy management because centralized and distributed MPC have been implemented for an electrified geared turbofan with accommodations for TEEM, and hierarchical MPC research is addressing supervisory energy management.

For failures, STARC-ABL reversionary logic updates the power-lever-angle and acceleration schedules to maintain geared-turbofan compressor operability and symmetric acceleration; geared-turbofan reversion modes also update variable-bleed-valve schedules for low-pressure-compressor operability and fuel-controller schedules for high-pressure-compressor operability and symmetric acceleration.

response.answer: The 16 electric engines—eight under each wing—are each supplied by an independent, fully redundant electrical power system. Four EPSs include both high-pressure- and low-pressure-shaft motor/generators. Secondary rechargeable batteries decouple electric-engine operation from the geared turbofan and enable independent throttle control; primary non-rechargeable batteries provide backup in the event of engine failure. The EPS model updates included revised component efficiencies, updated battery models, a DC-bus time constant made consistent with the turbomachinery timestep, and representation of the TCC as back-to-back inverter and rectifier.

claims.text: The SUSAN concept has 16 electric engines, with eight mounted under each wing, and each electric engine has an independent, fully redundant EPS; four EPSs include both HPS and LPS motor/generators.

Secondary rechargeable batteries decouple electric-engine and geared-turbofan operation and enable independent throttle control, while primary non-rechargeable batteries are used in case of engine failure.

The EPS model was updated with revised component efficiencies, updated battery models, a DC-bus time constant consistent with the turbomachinery model timestep, and a TCC modeled as back-to-back inverter and rectifier.

response.answer: Ti serpentine temperature sensors are fabricated directly on battery-separator material using shadow-mask or photoresist processing, with Ti selected for durability in battery chemistry. The serpentine resistor pattern is formed with extended leads to the separator edge, and lead wires are attached by wedge bonding. For pouch-cell integration, the sensor-bearing separator is placed between the anode and cathode, the pouch is sealed with electrolyte, and the leads remain accessible outside the cell. The sensor response is measured through AC resistance/impedance and normally decreases with increasing temperature. Exterior heating can produce a slower, delayed interior response because the pouch may not be in thermal equilibrium. An internal thermal fault is distinguishable by a rapid, pronounced resistance change that occurs while the exterior temperature changes only slightly or the heating-bath temperature remains constant; in testing, such an excursion occurred in less than a minute and was later associated with a short circuit.

claims.text: Ti serpentine temperature sensors are fabricated on separator material using shadow-mask or photoresist processing. The pattern includes leads extending to the separator edge, and lead wires can be attached using standard wedge bonding; Ti was selected for durability in battery chemistry.

For integration into a pouch cell, the sensor-bearing separator is placed between the anode and cathode, the pouch is sealed with electrolyte, and the thin-film sensor is connected to exterior leads, enabling interior monitoring during cycling.
The sensor is characterized by measuring AC resistance or impedance, and its baseline resistance decreases with increasing temperature, showing thermistor-like behavior.

During exterior heating, the pouch exterior and interior can respond at different rates because thermal equilibrium may be delayed; the interior sensor resistance nevertheless tracks the interior temperature change.

An internal thermal fault can be distinguished from slower exterior heating by a rapid, marked resistance change while the exterior temperature changes only slightly or the heating bath remains constant. A tested excursion was detected in less than a minute, and later evaluation suggested a short circuit as the cause.

response.answer: CFE-BNNS was mixed directly into the PAA precursor and ultrasonicated in an ice bath for 15–30 minutes before casting and thermal imidization. Morphologically, CFE-BNNS had thinner layers (about 2–10 nm), fewer layers, smaller BN particle sizes, and therefore higher surface area than CE-BNNS, whose layers were about 20–50 nm and showed vertically stacked nanosheets. BNNTs were cylindrical fillers with diameters of about 20–50 nm and micron-scale lengths. BNNT and CE-BNNS surfaces were functionalized with APTES to improve PAA dispersion by reducing agglomeration and minimizing van der Waals forces. In the unfunctionalized systems, CE-BNNS showed precipitation soon after addition to PAA, whereas BNNT initially achieved acceptable dispersion; however, increasing BNNT loading rapidly raised viscosity, making dispersion difficult. Particulate agglomeration was also observed after casting.

response.answer: HyPER and NEAT address complementary development scales and test objectives. HyPER supports lower-power, real-time control development and hardware-in-the-loop testing, with 100 kW, 400 V, bidirectional power flow and the ability to emulate turbomachinery or a general load. NEAT then extends validation to end-to-end, megawatt-scale electrified-aircraft powertrains, including high-power dynamometer testing and operation under simulated altitudes up to 60,000 feet. Together, they enable control and subsystem concepts to be developed and exercised on HyPER before integrated powertrains and propulsion units are tested at representative power and altitude in NEAT.

claims.text: HyPER is designed for real-time control testing and aeronautic propulsion-controls hardware-in-the-loop testing, with a maximum power of 100 kW, 400 V operation, bidirectional power flow, and turbomachinery or general-load emulation.

NEAT is designed for end-to-end development and testing of the electric portion of megawatt-scale electrified-aircraft powertrain systems and has a reconfigurable architecture for further technology maturation.

NEAT provides substantially higher-power validation capabilities, including a 1 MW electrical dynamometer, a 3.3 MW mechanical dynamometer, up to 3.75 MW of electrical power, and potential power levels up to 12 MW or more when regenerating.

NEAT can perform powertrain testing in an altitude environment corresponding to pressures up to 60,000 feet, including multi-kilovolt, megawatt testing with dual electric dynamometers inside an altitude chamber.

Thus, HyPER can support early control, emulation, and hardware-in-the-loop development, while NEAT can support later integrated, megawatt-scale and altitude-representative validation; the evidence establishes these complementary capabilities, though it does not specify a formal mandated test sequence between the facilities.

response.answer: For the electric quadrotor, the design-variable values were: rotor-support weight per unit length—baseline 7.5 lb/ft, sensitivity range 2.5–15 lb/ft; systems and equipment weight—baseline fixed weight 480 lb, sensitivity −200 to +200 lb relative to baseline; airframe drag increment ΔD/q—baseline 0 ft², sensitivity −2.0 to +2.0 ft²; main-rotor design blade loading CW/σ—baseline 0.09, sensitivity 0.07–0.09; rotor profile power—baseline 100%, sensitivity 80–100%; and motor weight factor—baseline 1.0, sensitivity 0.8–1.2.

claims.text: Rotor-support weight per unit length used a 7.5 lb/ft baseline and was varied from 2.5 to 15 lb/ft. Systems and equipment weight used a 480 lb baseline and was varied by −200 to +200 lb relative to that baseline.
Airframe drag increment ΔD/q was varied from −2.0 to +2.0 ft², with the zero increment representing the baseline.
Main-rotor design blade loading CW/σ used a 0.09 baseline and was varied down to 0.07; rotor profile power used a 100% baseline and was varied from 80% to 100%.
The electric motor weight factor was varied from 0.8 to 1.2 of the baseline, corresponding to a baseline factor of 1.0.

Simon Intelligent Control and Autonomy Branch NASA Glenn Research Center Cleveland, Ohio, USA donald.l.simon@nasa.gov Abstract— The augmentation of aircraft powertrains with electrical power systems is a promising path to reducing aircraft fuel consumption, emissions, and noise. Like conventional propulsion systems, electrified aircraft propulsion (EAP) systems will be subject to wear and tear throughout their lifecycles. System health management for EAP will enable efficient flight and maintenance scheduling, realizing economic, safety, and reliability benefits. A digital twin is, broadly, a dynamically updated virtual representation of an individual physical asset. This paper presents a Kalman filter-based approach for the development of a digital twin for an electrified powertrain and applies the approach to an EAP controls testbed. Measurements from nominal testbed operations are used to update a nonlinear model of the testbed. A Kalman filter is then created and used to identify and isolate anomalous testbed behavior based on measurements from off- nominal operations. Results show that the Kalman filter-based digital twin can monitor individual powertrain components’ health for degradation or other changes in performance. The applicability of the presented digital twin approach to any hybrid- or fully-electrified powertrain is emphasized. VII. CONCLUSIONS This paper presents a Kalman filter-based approach for constructing a digital twin of an electrified powertrain. A digital twin in this context is, broadly, a dynamically updated virtual representation of a specific physical asset. The digital twin identified minor, expected differences between a nonlinear testbed model and nominal test data acquired from the physical system. This structure reflected the assumption that measurement noise was independent across sensors. The process covariance matrix, Q, was designed as a scaled identity matrix, reflecting the assumptions that process noise was independent for all state variables and that the state variables were of similar magnitudes.
